games.explanation: Sean Burke is a walk machine masquerading as a strikeout arm, and the market keeps pricing him like the good half shows up on the road. Detroit runs out a righty-heavy order that fits his weakness perfectly, since Burke's numbers against right-handed bats collapse into an 11.7% barrel rate and double-digit walks. Jobe isn't a finished product either, but he's the better arm in this game and Chicago's lineup doesn't punish anyone in particular. Getting a plus price on the better team, the better starter, and the better matchup up and down the card is the entire ballgame. +126 on the Tigers is the side.

Nobody wants to back the Giants against Skubal, which is exactly why the number got this fat. The thing is, Skubal is human against right-handed bats in a way the reputation doesn't quite capture, and the Giants happen to run a lineup that leans right where it matters. Add a park that plays down for runs but juices the occasional mistake over the fence, and you have the ingredients for the kind of low-scoring, one-swing game where the underdog cashes more than a quarter of the time. The sim has this landing inside a run, and the market is paying you like it's a Dodgers formality. +320 on a coin flip that's closer to 3-to-2 is the entire ballgame.

Peralta is the kind of strikeout arm that looks scarier on paper than in a one-run game, and Boston getting a run and a half against a lineup this thin is the whole point. The right-handers at the top of the Sox order have been the exact profile that gives Peralta trouble, and Roman Anthony in particular has been punishing righties at a .412 xwOBA clip that plays anywhere. Tampa's counter is Yandy, Caminero, and a lot of hoping, which is not the profile of a team that routinely wins by four. The sim lands on a one-run game, the market is pricing a comfortable Rays win, and -185 on the cushion is the bet that splits the difference.

Yankees at home against a rookie starter is exactly the kind of line the market inflates on reputation, and the run line is where that overpricing shows up. Cam Schlittler is not the shutdown arm his ERA suggests, walking nearly a batter every ten faced and coughing up hard contact to righties at a rate that plays right into Marte and Perdomo at the top of this order. Pfaadt is the worse pitcher, nobody's disputing that, but the sim still lands on a one-run game because Arizona's lineup travels better than the board is treating it. Getting +1.5 at a reasonable price on a projected 4.7 to 4.3 fight is the whole ballgame. Take the runs and let the Yankees prove they can pull away.

Skubal is the best pitcher on the planet right now, which is exactly why the Giants only need to lose by a run to cash this ticket. The market is pricing this like Los Angeles takes batting practice off whoever San Francisco runs out there, but the sim lands on a tight 5-4 game where both bullpens do most of the work. Skubal's numbers actually flatten out against righties, and San Francisco happens to run a lineup that leans that way, with Jung Hoo Lee posting a .342 xwOBA versus right-handed arms as the guy asked to keep the line moving. Plus money on a game the projection calls a one-run coin flip is the kind of price you take and stop asking questions.
